description: I'm a designer interested in making some easy to use interfaces for this challenge, and I am based in Mountain View. I am open to teammates who want to learn together. I plan to use Claude for this project.
summary:
...To the Moon! is a browser-based planner for choosing when and where to land near the lunar south pole. Pick a site and date to see when the Sun is up for power, when Earth is visible for direct communication, and when NASA’s Deep Space Network can reach the site.

Features: side-by-side site comparison (Artemis III candidate regions, IM-1, IM-2, Blue Ghost, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang’e 4/6, Apollo 11-17, or any dropped pin); a 360° horizon view with the Sun and Earth at true size; a shaded-relief south polar map; a year-ahead calendar that suggests the best 7-day window; landing-slip scenarios; and a sensitivity readout (at Shackleton ridge, a 2° higher horizon cuts sunlight from 100% to 3%). Plain-language tooltips make it usable for educators and the public.

How it works: Sun and Earth positions are computed for each site and time, then checked against real terrain horizons from NASA’s LOLA south pole elevation model (LDEM_60S_240MPP_ADJ). The horizons are traced every 2° of azimuth out to 450 km, accounting for the Moon’s curvature. The data is precomputed and built into the page, so it runs in any browser.

Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python and the open-source Astronomy Engine library. Results are planning-level, and Artemis III coordinates are approximate.
details:
What it does:

  • Compares landing sites side by side: Artemis III candidate regions, NASA commercial landers (IM-1, IM-2, Blue Ghost), international missions (Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang’e 4 and 6) and Apollo 11 to 17. Users can also drop a pin anywhere.
  • Shows a 360° horizon view from each site, with the Sun and Earth drawn at true size against the real terrain.
  • Includes a south polar map in shaded relief, with arrows pointing toward the Sun and Earth.
  • Has a year-ahead calendar that shades each day by sunlight, Earth visibility or operations windows (Sun + Earth + DSN all available) and suggests the best 7-day stretch.
  • Has “what if landing slips” scenarios showing how results change if the date moves.
  • Shows a sensitivity readout for how sunlight drops if the surrounding ridge were 1°, 2° or 3° higher.
  • Includes plain-language explainers (ⓘ buttons and hover tooltips) so students and the public can follow along.

How it works:
Sun and Earth positions are computed for each site and time, then checked against that site’s terrain horizon. Horizons come from NASA’s LOLA south pole elevation model. For each site we traced rays every 2° of azimuth out to 450 km, accounting for the Moon’s curvature, with the observer 2 m above the ground. That precomputed data is built into the page, so it runs offline in any browser.

Tools and languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python (data processing), Astronomy Engine (open-source ephemeris library), IAU lunar orientation model.

Limits: 240 m pixels miss boulders and small slopes, so results are planning-level. NASA has not published exact Artemis III site coordinates, so those are approximate and labeled “approx.” in the tool.
dataRefs: LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) south pole elevation model, LDEM_60S_240MPP_ADJ (Barker et al.), from NASA Goddard’s Planetary Geodesy Data Archive (PGDA): https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/products/90. Used to compute real terrain horizons for every site and the shaded-relief polar map. NASA Deep Space Network: antenna site locations (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra) used to model when Earth stations can see the Moon. Published landing coordinates for NASA CLPS missions and Apollo landing sites.

NASA Deep Space Network (JPL): https://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/ Locations of NASA’s three DSN antenna complexes (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra). Used to model when Earth stations can communicate with each site.
NASA JPL Horizons System: https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/ NASA’s solar system ephemeris service. It’s the reference that Astronomy Engine’s Sun and Moon positions are validated against.
